evidence.claim: General Prayut Chan-o-cha is listed as the 29th Prime Minister, with Term 2 running from 2019-07-09 to 2023-09-04.
evidence.title: Cabinet Directory
evidence.excerpt: General Prayut Chan-o-cha is listed as the 29th Prime Minister, with Term 2 running from 2019-07-09 to 2023-09-04.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official government roster with tenure dates.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the 2022 period and anchors office identity.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct office record for Prayut Chan-o-cha.
contrary_evidence: Office identity alone does not show any nuclear or existential-risk decision-making.

evidence.claim: Section 158 says the King appoints the Prime Minister on House approval, the Council of Ministers acts by collective responsibility, and the Prime Minister cannot hold office for more than eight years in total.
evidence.title: Constitution of the Kingdom of Thailand B.E. 2560 (2017)
evidence.publisher: Office of the Council of State via CYRILLA
evidence.excerpt: Section 158 says the King appoints the Prime Minister on House approval, the Council of Ministers acts by collective responsibility, and the Prime Minister cannot hold office for more than eight years in total.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional text from an official legal translation repository.
evidence.period_fit: Sets the constitutional authority and hard constraint in force during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Defines the institutional limits of Prayut's office rather than a personal nuclear mandate.
contrary_evidence: This is general executive authority, not nuclear-specific authority.

evidence.claim: Freedom House said Thailand’s regime used authoritarian tactics in 2022, including arbitrary arrests, intimidation, lèse-majesté charges, and harassment of activists, and that the emergency decree used to limit public assembly expired in October 2022 after being used to quash dissent.
evidence.title: Thailand: Freedom in the World 2023 Country Report
evidence.excerpt: Freedom House said Thailand’s regime used authoritarian tactics in 2022, including arbitrary arrests, intimidation, lèse-majesté charges, and harassment of activists, and that the emergency decree used to limit public assembly expired in October 2022 after being used to quash dissent.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Well-known independent country report summarizing 2022 rights conditions.
evidence.period_fit: Directly describes 2022 conditions and the October 2022 decree expiration.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Prayut’s government, not to a single isolated local official.
contrary_evidence: The same report notes a somewhat more open political environment in the Bangkok governor race, so the picture is not total closure.

evidence.claim: HRW said the Prayut government continued to restrict fundamental rights in 2022 and that at least 1,860 people had been prosecuted since mid-2020 for expression and assembly, including at least 1,469 under the Emergency Decree, with most cases not dropped after the emergency ended.
evidence.title: Thailand: Rights Repressed
evidence.excerpt: HRW said the Prayut government continued to restrict fundamental rights in 2022 and that at least 1,860 people had been prosecuted since mid-2020 for expression and assembly, including at least 1,469 under the Emergency Decree, with most cases not dropped after the emergency ended.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent annual report with explicit 2022 coverage and quantified prosecution data.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 and the post-repeal persistence of cases.
contrary_evidence: The same period also produced the torture/enforced-disappearance bill, so the year mixed repression with some reform.

evidence.claim: HRW said Thai riot police used apparently excessive force against APEC protesters on 18 November 2022, beating demonstrators and firing rubber bullets, and urged Prime Minister Prayut to order an impartial investigation.
evidence.title: Thailand: Police Forcibly Disperse APEC Protesters
evidence.excerpt: HRW said Thai riot police used apparently excessive force against APEC protesters on 18 November 2022, beating demonstrators and firing rubber bullets, and urged Prime Minister Prayut to order an impartial investigation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous independent reporting with witness review and injury allegations.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tied to a major protest-policing event.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly names Prayut’s government as responsible for the policing response.
contrary_evidence: HRW notes protesters tried to push through police barricades, so the event was contested rather than one-sided.

evidence.claim: Thai PBS reported that APEC protest injuries led participants to file complaints against police, that some protesters were hit by rubber bullets, and that rights groups and the National Human Rights Commission called for an investigation.
evidence.title: ผู้บาดเจ็บจากชุมนุม ราษฎรหยุด APEC 2022 แจ้งความเอาผิดตำรวจ
evidence.excerpt: Thai PBS reported that APEC protest injuries led participants to file complaints against police, that some protesters were hit by rubber bullets, and that rights groups and the National Human Rights Commission called for an investigation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous local-language reporting with injury details and official/rights reactions.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tied to APEC protest policing.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State policing under Prayut’s government; the report also notes police claims that protesters violated conditions.
contrary_evidence: Police said officers were injured and that they needed force for self-defense, so the event is contested.

evidence.claim: Amnesty said Thailand’s crackdown on child protesters involved intimidation, surveillance, and criminalization, and it estimated that 283 protesters under 18 had been charged since 2020, with nearly 200 cases still active in late 2022.
evidence.title: Thailand: Authorities must drop charges against child protesters
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty said Thailand’s crackdown on child protesters involved intimidation, surveillance, and criminalization, and it estimated that 283 protesters under 18 had been charged since 2020, with nearly 200 cases still active in late 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent rights organization with specific quantified allegations and contemporaneous timing.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and focused on the lingering effects of protest repression.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thai authorities under Prayut’s government.
contrary_evidence: The repeal of the emergency decree later in 2022 reduced one legal basis, but Amnesty says the cases remained active.

evidence.claim: Amnesty reported that at least 1,468 people in 661 protest-related cases had been charged or prosecuted under the Emergency Decree from May 2020 to September 2022, including at least 241 children, and that 574 cases were still ongoing after repeal.
evidence.title: Thai officials must drop all the ongoing prosecutions under the Emergency Decree
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty reported that at least 1,468 people in 661 protest-related cases had been charged or prosecuted under the Emergency Decree from May 2020 to September 2022, including at least 241 children, and that 574 cases were still ongoing after repeal.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Detailed local rights-monitoring analysis with quantified case totals and repeal context.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the 2022 repeal period and its aftermath.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government-wide legal practice under Prayut, not a single incident.
contrary_evidence: The government did repeal the decree by late 2022, which is a partial restraint signal.

evidence.claim: Thai PBS reported that Thailand’s nationwide COVID emergency decree and related orders were repealed effective 1 October 2022, while the severe emergency in the southern border provinces remained in force.
evidence.title: ราชกิจจาฯ ประกาศยกเลิก พ.ร.ก.ฉุกเฉิน มีผล 1 ต.ค.นี้
evidence.excerpt: Thai PBS reported that Thailand’s nationwide COVID emergency decree and related orders were repealed effective 1 October 2022, while the severe emergency in the southern border provinces remained in force.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous local-language reporting from a major Thai outlet reproducing the official repeal notice.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and exactly relevant to emergency-power use.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The repeal notice was issued by the acting prime minister on behalf of the government, reflecting Prayut-era governance rather than a personal crisis act.
contrary_evidence: The southern-border emergency remained, so emergency governance did not disappear entirely.

evidence.claim: OHCHR said the new torture and enforced-disappearance law was a major step toward zero tolerance and legal redress, but that Thailand still had 76 unresolved disappearance cases and needed further amendments for full compliance.
evidence.title: NEWS RELEASE: UN Human Rights Office welcomes Thailand’s enactment of the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearances Act
evidence.publisher: OHCHR Regional Office for South-East Asia
evidence.excerpt: OHCHR said the new torture and enforced-disappearance law was a major step toward zero tolerance and legal redress, but that Thailand still had 76 unresolved disappearance cases and needed further amendments for full compliance.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN human-rights monitoring statement on a new Thai law and the remaining gap.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and directly relevant to accountability for abuse.
evidence.ruler_attribution: A state legal reform under Prayut’s government, not a personal police order.
contrary_evidence: OHCHR explicitly says key provisions still need amendment, so the reform is important but incomplete.

evidence.claim: The UK welcomed Thailand’s progress on the torture/disappearance bill but warned that draft NGO and media laws could damage civic space and urged Thailand to protect fundamental freedoms and human-rights defenders.
evidence.title: UN Human Rights Council 49: UK statement for the Universal Periodic Review Adoption - Thailand
evidence.excerpt: The UK welcomed Thailand’s progress on the torture/disappearance bill but warned that draft NGO and media laws could damage civic space and urged Thailand to protect fundamental freedoms and human-rights defenders.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official foreign-government statement in a multilateral rights review.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tied to Thailand’s human-rights governance record.
evidence.ruler_attribution: External state assessment of the Prayut government, not a direct domestic operational record.
contrary_evidence: It is an outside statement, so it is weaker than Thai official records for formal legal acts.

evidence.claim: After the October 2022 daycare massacre that killed 37 people, mostly children, Prayut ordered a crackdown on drugs, emphasized rehabilitation, and directed police and provincial governors to strengthen drug-prevention plans.
evidence.title: Thai PM announces crackdown on drugs in wake of nursery attack
evidence.excerpt: After the October 2022 daycare massacre that killed 37 people, mostly children, Prayut ordered a crackdown on drugs, emphasized rehabilitation, and directed police and provincial governors to strengthen drug-prevention plans.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous international reporting with direct attribution to Prayut and the government spokesperson.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tied to a major domestic violence crisis.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributes the response to Prayut and his government.
contrary_evidence: The shooter was a former police officer, so this event also exposes security-force failure rather than only ordinary criminality.

unresolved_gaps: No Prayut-specific 2022 nuclear or other existential-risk choice is evidenced; the package is mostly inherited treaty and safeguards context.
No direct cabinet-minute or NSC record ties Prayut personally to each 2022 Ukraine or Myanmar diplomatic position.
Direct command-chain evidence for specific police operations, protest policing, and protest-prosecution decisions is limited.
Direct documentary proof of Prayut's personal authorization of spyware or surveillance is absent.
Ruler-level evidence on appointments quality and 2022 rule-setting for competition, property rights, and investment remains thin.
Outcome evidence is stronger than direct ruler attribution across health, education, and social protection.
No direct 2022 evidence of hidden assets, family profit, or proven deception beyond disclosure opacity and allegations.
There is no single consolidated FY2022 execution audit tying the program, implementation, and outcomes back to Prayut's full cabinet-level agenda.
